Industry observers note that third, to define an internal control region and identify mWmC-positive cells in each section, we implemented automated identification of the control region and quantification of mWmC+ cells. In this pipeline, we used an automated depth-aware sliding-window analysis. For each cell i, the locally background-corrected fluorescence intensity was summarized by the mean pixel intensity within the soma’s inner measurement ring after local background subtraction, as described above. Cell centroids were computed from the segmentation mask, and a sliding window of height 800 µm was moved along the pial-to-deep axis in 100-µm increments. Within each window w, we computed the cumulative fluorescence energy as \({S}_{w}=\sum _{i\in w}{I}_{i},\) where Ii is the per-cell fluorescence metric (post-subtraction inner ring mean intensity in this case). Windows with fewer than 15 cells were excluded. The resulting curve Sw versus depth was smoothed with a seven-point moving average, and the valley (minimum) among valid windows was selected as the centre of the control region, corresponding to the zone of lowest cumulative signal (background). From this valley, the control region was symmetrically expanded until at least 600 cells were included. The final control region was exported as a rectangular ROI spanning the full mediolateral width. For all cells within the control ROI, Ii were aggregated to estimate the control population mean (μctrl) and standard deviation (σctrl). We then defined mWmC+ cells using the below threshold: after trimming the top 2% of brightest cells to exclude outliers confounded by, for example, neighbouring overexposed pixels, thresholds for positive detection were defined as T5σ = μctrl + 5σctrl as the baseline to register mWmC+ cells.

Sources indicate that finally, with the per-cell mWmC information, we further assigned a cell type as mWmC+ (retino-recipient) by first deriving the mWmC+ cell profiles across different cell types using the methods described above. Encouragingly, automatically assigned mWmC+ cell profiles correlate strongly with manual annotations, indicating consistency across methods. To quantify enrichment of mWmC+ cells across neuronal subtypes, we computed an enrichment score for each tracing and cell type using the following steps. For each tracing × cell type, we constructed a 2 × 2 table of mWmC+ and mWmC− counts inside the cell type versus all other cells and applied a one-tailed Fisher’s exact test (alternative = “greater”). The odds ratio (OR) was computed as:.

In a recent development, where a and b are the numbers of mWmC+ and mWmC− cells within the given subtype, and c and d are the corresponding counts outside that subtype. The effect size was visualized as log2(OR) (values < 0 clipped to 0). At the same time, statistical evidence was encoded by a point area proportional to −log10(P). Cell types with positive enrichment (log2(OR) > 0) were highlighted with a red outline (Fig. 2o). We assign a cell type as positive or connected under a specific tracing condition when the log2(OR) value is greater than 0 (enrichment). Based on the mWmC+ cell types assigned here, we summarized the mean mWmC+ cell proportion across animals (error bar: s.e.m.) as bar plots (Figs. 1k and 3c).

In a recent development, the neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. To determine parameters better reflect internal data structure and cell-type granularity, we chose clustering parameters based on statistical assessment and established parameter selection tools. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. The parameter selections here allowed us to settle on a granularity of cell types that best represent the internal data structure in an unbiased way. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below. Subsequent comparisons to published SC atlas showed high consistency, for example, when compared to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain Atlas at supertype level, supporting the robustness of selected parameters and the resulting granularity of cell types.

To perform clustering and dimension reduction, we first applied SCTransform-based normalization67 to the expression matrix for each MERFISH section. This was enabled by accessing the SCTransform algorithm implemented in the R package via rpy2 from Python. Prior to normalization, raw counts were stored in adata.layers[‘raw_counts’]. A quality control filtering step was then applied to remove low-quality features, retaining genes detected in at least 5 cells (sc.pp.filter_genes) and cells with a total count of at least 5 (sc.pp.filter_cells). After filtering, the sparse matrices were explicitly sorted to ensure compatibility. Each AnnData object was converted to a Seurat object (as.Seurat()), and SCTransform was applied (do.correct.umi = FALSE). SCTransform models sequencing depth (library size/total unique molecular identifiers (UMIs)) as a technical covariate during normalization. The full set of normalized gene expression values was extracted from the SCT assay’s scale.data slot and stored in adata.layers[‘normalized’], ensuring that any genes missing post-normalization were reintroduced as zero-filled vectors to retain consistency with the original feature set. The normalized matrix was then assigned to adata.X for downstream analysis. Raw counts were preserved in adata.raw, and standard quality control metrics (n_genes_by_counts, total_counts) were computed using the raw layer. Based on the quality control metrics, two sections with low quality and significantly lower counts were excluded from further analysis.

The AnnDatas of the remaining MERFISH slices were subsequently merged using scanpy (v1.10.4; abbreviated as sc onwards) with ad.concat (merge = ‘unique’, index_unique=None), yielding a combined dataset of 47,740 cells. Cell identifiers were made unique across slices, and principal component analysis was performed on the merged expression matrix (sc.tl.pca). The variance explained by each component was examined to guide dimensionality reduction (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). A neighbourhood graph was constructed using the top 15 principal components (n_pcs = 15) and 30 nearest neighbours (n_neighbors = 30) by sc.pp.neighbors. UMAP was then applied for two-dimensional embedding (sc.tl.umap). Unsupervised clustering was carried out using the Leiden algorithm with a resolution parameter of 0.8 (sc.tl.leiden). We examined the distribution of quality control metrics across the clusters. We found high consistency of n_genes_by_counts and total_counts across clusters except lower detection rate in one cluster (Extended Data Fig. 1h), which was identified as non-neuronal cells via the SC XGBoost classifier as described above (Extended Data Fig. 1i). To improve classification resolution, the non-neuronal cluster was excluded, yielding 46,277 high-quality transcriptomic profiles for neuronal cells. The neuronal subset was re-clustered using a similar framework as described above. Principal component dimensionality (n_pcs = 12) was selected based on inspection of the variance explained curve (sc.pl.pca_variance_ratio). Clustering resolution was subsequently determined using the clustering tree approach implemented in the clustree R package to assess cluster stability across multiple resolutions, and a resolution of 1.5 was selected. These clusters were then labelled using the approaches described below.

In a recent development, to robustly identify the molecular identity of the above-identified MERFISH clusters, we took the following steps to classify the identified clusters and compare them to established SC atlases: first, we examined the gene expression pattern for a set of SC canonical marker genes (Fig. 1g) and the dendrogram between these clusters based on hierarchical clustering of averaged expression per cluster (sc.tl.dendrogram). Second, we aligned our MERFISH data to the 10x Whole Mouse Brain (CCN20230722) taxonomy30 using the MapMyCells tool suite from the Allen Institute. Third, we utilized the XGBoost classifier, as described above, to link the MERFISH data to our and other published SC scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq neuron-type atlases6,27,28, using the shared genes between the MERFISH panel and the snRNA-seq genes as features (Extended Data Fig. 2c,g,j). Finally, we compared the expression pattern of key marker genes between our data and previously published SC datasets (Extended Data Fig. 2d). Overall, the identified clusters captured the neuronal diversity of the SC at high resolution, demonstrating strong concordance—and in some cases, enhanced granularity—compared to established reference atlases.

In a recent development, we implemented a sublaminar-controlled cell-type specificity analysis to test the specificity of each SC type in specifying the connections with presynaptic RGC inputs (Fig. 2d). The analysis is based on a permutation-based statistical framework with Stouffer z-score aggregation across mice. More specifically, to assess cell-type–specific enrichment or depletion of mWmC+ labelling independent of sublaminar distribution, we performed a sublaminar-controlled permutation test. Within each mouse, SC neurons were binned by soma depth (50 µm unless otherwise specified). Within each (animal × depth bin) stratum, cell-type labels were randomly shuffled, thereby preserving the sublaminar distribution of mWmC labelling while disrupting the association between cell-type identity and mWmC labelling. All permutation tests were performed with 1,000 permutations using a fixed random seed unless otherwise stated. For each permutation, we computed the number of mWmC+ cells per cell type, yielding a null distribution of expected counts under the hypothesis that sublaminar position alone explains connectivity. Observed mWmC+ cell counts were then converted into per-animal z-scores relative to this null distribution. Specifically, for each cell type t and mouse q, the z-score was computed as follows,.

Recent findings suggest that where \({N}_{t,q}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes the observed number of mWmC+ cells of type t in mouse q, and μt,q and σt,q denote the mean and standard deviation of the permutation-derived null distribution for that cell type and mouse. z-Scores provide a signed, normalized measure of enrichment or depletion relative to sublaminar expectation. z-Scores were then aggregated across mice using Stouffer’s method as below,.

where n is the number of mice. To test for bidirectional deviations (enrichment or depletion) of mWmC labelling beyond sublaminar expectation, two-sided P values were computed from the combined z-scores using the standard normal distribution as,.

Recent findings suggest that and controlled for multiple comparisons across cell types using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Positive z-scores indicate enrichment beyond sublaminar expectation, whereas negative z-scores indicate depletion, reflecting cases in which sublaminar position alone overestimates the likelihood of receiving retinal input. As statistical inference is performed using normal-theory P values derived from the aggregated z-scores (after estimating null mean and variance from permutations), the minimum attainable P value is not constrained by the number of permutations. Finally, SC neuron types were ranked by their aggregated Stouffer z-scores, which we refer to as the cell-type specificity score, representing the preference of a cell type’s molecular identity for RGC connectivity (Fig. 2e).

In a recent development, RGC axons in the SC from four different genotypes and all RGCs were included. In brief, coronal brain sections were immunostained and imaged using a confocal microscope, as previously described43. Confocal stacks of 20 µm thickness were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Using ImageJ, each right SC hemisphere was divided into five equal sections. The fluorescence profile of axon arbors was measured by taking 200-μm-thick line scans perpendicular to each section’s pial surface, extending to a depth of 500 μm below it. Signal intensity values were normalized to the maximum intensity across images and plotted. The locally weighted scatterplot smoothing function in MATLAB was used to smooth the curve. To quantify axon depth across the SC, the shortest distance from the pial surface to the upper and lower boundaries of the axonal arbors was measured within each section. For experiments in which multiple neurons were recorded from the same mouse, mouse identity was treated as the experimental unit/random effect to account for the hierarchical structure of the data.

It has been revealed that the retina histology protocol was described as previously described50. Mice were euthanized, and eyes were collected, then fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 1 h on ice. Retinas were dissected and rinsed with PBS. For the whole-mount retina data in Fig. 3, we adapted previously described protocols37. Whole-mount retina samples were blocked in blocking buffer (5% normal donkey serum, 0.5% Triton X-100 in PBS) at room temperature for 1 h, then incubated with primary antibodies for 2–4 days at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 2 h at room temperature. For mounting, retinas were placed flat, ganglion cell side up, and sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech, 0100-01). For retinal vertical sections in Extended Data Fig. 6, we adapted protocols previously described37. Fixed mouse retinas were cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS for 1 h before embedding in OCT (Epredia). Vertical retinal cryosections (20 µm) were prepared and mounted on glass slides. Sections were blocked in the same blocking buffer and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were sealed with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

Brain section histology was described previously68. Mice were deeply anaesthetized and perfused transcardially with ice-cold PBS, followed by 4% PFA. Brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 °C, then cryoprotected in 30% sucrose in PBS at 4 °C until the tissue blocks sank. Tissue was frozen directly on the stage of a sliding microtome (Leica) cooled with dry ice and sectioned coronally at 40 µm. Free-floating sections were blocked in the blocking buffer described above and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, then for 1 h at room temperature with secondary antibodies. Sections were mounted on slides with Fluoromount-G (SouthernBiotech) containing DAPI.

Antibodies used were as follows: goat and chicken anti-GFP (1:1,000, Rockland; 1:500, Abcam); rabbit anti-RFP (1:1,000, Rockland for immunohistochemistry); mouse anti-SATB1 (marker for ooDSGC in reference69, 1:1,000, Santa Cruz); goat anti-choline acetyltransferase (ChAT, 1:500, Millipore); rabbit anti-CARTPT (1:2,500, Phoenix Pharmaceuticals); rabbit anti-TUSC5 (1:500, Novus); Rabbit anti-RBPMS (1:1,000, Poteintech/Fisher); goat anti-SPP1 (1:500, R&D); sheep anti-FOXP2 (1:500, R&D); rabbit anti-ETV1 (1:1,000, J.A.K.)70. Secondary antibodies were conjugated to Alexa Fluor 488, Alexa Fluor 568, or Alexa Fluor 647 (Jackson ImmunoResearch) and used at 1:1,000.

In situ hybridization was performed as previously described68 using RNAscope Fluorescent Multiplex Kit (Advanced Cell Diagnostics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. In brief, sections were fixed in 4% PFA and dehydrated as described in ‘Immunohistochemistry for the retina and SC’, followed by air drying. A hydrophobic barrier was drawn around the sections with an ImmEdge pen (Vector Labs, H-4000). The sections were post-fixed with 4% PFA, quenched with hydrogen peroxide, and subjected to target retrieval followed by dehydration in 100% ethanol. Sections were treated with Protease III, incubated with target probes, treated with a series of amplification reagents, and developed with TSA fluorophores. Slides were mounted using mounting medium (VECTASHIELD, Vector Laboratories). RNAscope probes included the following: Cdh7 (ACD #521331), Cbln4 (ACD #505411), Itga7 (ACD #542911) and Sntb1 (ACD #440541).

For optogenetic experiments, AAV2-CAG-ChR2-mCherry-WPRE, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV2-EF1α-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-mCherry were injected into the left eyes of mice to activate all RGCs or ooDSGCs. Mice were allowed to mature for at least 6 wpi, reaching adulthood (6–10 weeks) before analysis.

For starburst amacrine cell (Chat+) ablation experiments, AAV2-Flex-taCasp3-TEVp was injected into the left eye or both eyes of mice in the ablation groups. 2 sites located at the dorsal and ventral parts of the eyeball were used for injection; 0.75 µl of virus was injected into each site. For the control groups, same volume of saline was injected into the left eye of mice. Two-photon calcium imaging was performed 1 month after injection.

AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-mCherry or AAV2-EF1a-FDIO-EGFP (1 µl) was injected into the right SC of adult mice at a constant speed (60 nl min−1).

After 30 min incubation, the slices were transferred to room temperature artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF; 125 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.25 mM NaH2PO4, 26 mM NaHCO3, 1 mM MgCl2·6H2O, 2 mM CaCl2, 20 mM D-glucose, pH 7.4) before recording. Recent findings suggest that A CCD camera (IR-2000, DAGE-MTI) mounted on a fluorescence microscope (BX51WI, Olympus) was used to detect a green cell surrounded by red axon terminals. In vivo calcium imaging of mouse SC was performed using a two-photon microscope as previously described72.

According to recent reports, surgeries were performed on eight-week-old transgenic mice. The craniotomy, virus injection, and transparent silicone plug insertion were done over the right SC. Mice were anaesthetized with 2% isoflurane for maintenance and injected with meloxicam (5 mg kg−1). Craniotomy was performed over the lambda of the skull, and a large flap was opened in the dura with a forceps (Dumoxel-Biology 11252-30, FST). We injected the right SC with 400 nl of AAV8-EF1α-FDIO-GCaMP6s. A silicone plug bonded to a 5 mm circular coverslip was mounted on a suction cup and positioned over the craniotomy. The plug advanced downward to press the brain and then anteriorly to displace the dura and transverse sinuses. A custom head plate (titanium, 1 mm thick, eMachineShop) was bonded to the skull by cyanoacrylate (Vetbond, 3 M) and dental cement (Ortho-Jet, LangDental). At least 2 weeks after implanting cranial windows, mice were habituated to handling and head-fixing at least 4 times under a two-photon microscope.

In a recent development, we imaged calcium responses in mice using a two-photon microscope (Neurolabware) with a Spectra-Physics MaiTai laser at 920 nm (15–50 mW) to excite GCaMP6s. Imaging in the SC was performed at depths of 50–200 µm below the pia surface. A 575 × 370 µm field of view was scanned at 15.5 Hz, producing a series of 416 × 268-pixel images. A tangent LCD screen (Dell, U2312HM) placed in front of the left eye of head-fixed mice will present a visual stimulus generated with Psychtoolbox3 (MATLAB) and synchronized with image acquisition via TTL signals from the stimulus screen. The screen is centred 14 cm away from the mouse, angled at 20 degrees in pitch and yaw to minimize fisheye distortion. We imaged each mouse for about 1 h, with multiple sessions on successive days if needed to present a battery of visual stimuli and acquire stable imaging.

Visual stimuli were presented on a tangent (1,920 × 1,080 pixels) region of the screen. The screen was strobed for 2 µs at the end of each scan line (1,200 Hz; luminance of the grey screen, 1.25 cd m−2; maximum brightness, 1/80 of the unmodified monitor) to minimize interference between the visual stimulus and two-photon fluorescence detection. All stimuli presented used only the green and blue channels of the screen. Red bars flickered periodically at the bottom of the screen, which was covered with black tape, to convey the timing of the visual stimulus to synchronize with fluorescence acquisition. All visual stimuli in two-photon experiments were presented in a pseudorandom sequence, interspersed with blank periods within each stimulus block, using a different random seed for each block. Moving gratings were used to test the direction selectivity of SC neurons. The drifting grating was 100 pixels wide (6.4°), with black or white bars, and drifted in 8 directions (45° intervals) at a speed of 356 pixels per second (22.7° per second). To map receptive fields, flashing spots were presented in a 9 × 5 position arrayed across the stimulus monitor. Each spot was a 216 × 216 pixel (13.8° × 13.8°) square that appeared for 1 second. All visual stimuli were repeated six times per trial.

To test the contribution of the ipsilateral eye to the direction selectivity of Cbln4+ SC neurons, we covered the ipsilateral eye with a black box during calcium imaging. The box was removed after the experiments.

We performed offline motion correction of calcium imaging data by NoRMCorre73, identified GCaMP6s+ cells, extracted calcium traces for each cell, and subtracted neuropil signals. Next, we aligned traces to visual stimuli using synchronization pulses relayed from stimulus monitors to the microscope via a TTL signal, which were time-stamped in the imaging data. For traces with high-peak noisy spikes (large mouse motion that cannot be corrected), we used a denoising algorithm to replace noisy dots with smooth traces. The noisy spike traces were determined by whether any points were bigger than the mean ± 4 s.d. traces. Then, calcium traces were aligned to the onset of each visual stimulus, averaged across trials, and the peak and valley of each mean trace were identified.

DSI calculation followed a previously published protocol74. ΔF/F values for each presentation of a stimulus were averaged from six repeats, and the peak ΔF/F for each direction was used to compute direction preference. The direction selectivity index (DSI) was calculated as the normalized amplitude of the vector sum of all directions by their scalar sum. Cells with DSI > 0.2 were classified as direction selective. The preferred direction was defined as the weighted vector sum over eight stimulus angles.

Sources indicate that for confocal image acquisition, all procedures were conducted in a double-blind manner. One researcher collected images without knowledge of genotype, while a second researcher, who performed the analysis, was also blinded. Littermates were used as controls in all experiments unless otherwise indicated. Both male and female mice were included. Images were acquired on a Zeiss LSM900 confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss Microscopy) equipped with 10× air, 20× air and 40× oil immersion objectives.

To quantify immunostained cells in the SC and retina, confocal images of vertical retinal sections, coronal SC sections, and whole-mount retina were collected under identical imaging conditions across all samples. Confocal stacks of 20 µm (retina and SC sections) or 60 µm (whole-mount retina) were acquired and processed to generate maximum-intensity projections. Cells positive for each marker was identified using thresholded fluorescence intensity criteria. Single-positive and double-positive cells were manually counted with the Cell Counter plugin in ImageJ (NIH). For RNAscope in situ hybridization, SC sections processed with RNAscope and immunostaining were imaged on a Zeiss LSM900 with a 20× objective. The number of GFP-positive neurons or marker-positive cells was counted across all stained samples as mentioned above. Data were pooled across animals, and results are presented as percentages (mean ± s.e.m.). Confocal image files for histology were analysed using Fiji Image J (v1.53c), Microsoft Excel 365, Graph Pad Prism9, Adobe Illustrator 2020. Electrophysiological data collection and analysis were not performed blindly with respect to the experimental conditions. All whole-cell recording data were acquired by Camplex 10.7 (Molecular Devices) and analysed in MATLAB (MathWorks) or Clampfit 10.7 (Molecular Devices). Optogenetically evoked currents were averaged across 5 trials. Clampfit 10.7 measured the peak amplitudes of evoked currents. MATLAB analysed the intrinsic properties of recorded neurons. All statistics were calculated by GraphPad Prism 9. Peak currents between the two groups were compared using a two-tailed Student’s t-test.

Optomotor response was described previously75. The OptoDrum (Striatech) comprises a box with four screens to simulate drifting gratings. An IR camera mounted on the top of the box was used to record mouse movements. Mice were first acclimated to the room in their cages for 30 min. Then, freely moving mice were placed on a platform and allowed to acclimate to the box for at least 5 min. Drifting gratings (12° s−1) in the clockwise direction can trigger left-eye-mediated body and head movements, while drifting gratings in the counterclockwise direction were used to test right-eye-mediated movements. Drifting gratings were presented from low spatial frequencies (0.056 cycles per degree) to high frequencies (0.3–0.5 cycles per degree) to determine the threshold at which a mouse could track. OptoDrum’s software can detect the body shape of mice and label the positions of head, body, and tail of mice. The stimulus and video tracking were paused if a mouse engaged in grooming behaviour or dropped off the platform and resumed later. The software can score the optomotor response and determine the spatial-frequency threshold. False positives were manually identified as invalid, and the same frequency of drifting gratings was repeated. We compared the spatial-frequency threshold of drifting gratings to trigger optomotor responses in the left eye (ablation) with the right eye (control) to assess visual acuity differences.

It has been revealed that we obtained measurements from distinct biological samples. No covariates were tested. No formal test of normality was performed; statistical tests were selected based on the distributional assumptions of the data. Statistical methods and the number of animals tested for each configuration are documented in the figure legends for each experiment. When comparing two groups, statistics were derived using an unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test, Kolmogorov–Smirnov test or Fisher’s exact test, as indicated in the figure legends. For comparing cell-type proportions across multiple reactions, we used the Kruskal–Wallis H test (scipy.stats.kruskal, Python). One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed in GraphPad Prism 9 to assess the statistical significance of differences among multiple measurements.

Fisher’s exact test was performed using the Easy Fisher Exact Test Calculator (https://www.socscistatistics.com/tests/fisher/default2.aspx).

Recent findings suggest that statistical significance was defined as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001. All values indicate mean ± s.e.m., unless otherwise noted.

a, Unsupervised classification of sSC using the standard fresh-frozen MERFISH protocol. UMAP embedding of 5,845 cells reveals consistent clustering of the same 8 ENCs and 11 INCs identified with TransA-MERFISH on fixed tissue (Fig. 1d). Cell-type labels were assigned to Leiden clusters based on canonical marker gene expression patterns and transcriptomic mapping via a supervised XGBoost classifier trained on the TransA-MERFISH atlas. b, Confusion matrix showing transcriptomic correspondence between cell types in standard MERFISH (rows) and TransA-MERFISH (columns). c, Violin plots comparing quality control metrics between standard MERFISH (blue) and TransA-MERFISH (gray). Distributions are highly similar across key metrics, including the number of genes detected per cell (n_genes_by_counts), total transcript counts per cell (total_counts), and cell mask area (in pixels). A modest reduction in n_genes_by_counts and total_counts was observed in TransA-MERFISH experiments. d, Comparison of matched neuronal subtype frequencies between standard MERFISH and TransA-MERFISH. Values are plotted on a ln-ln scale to highlight low-frequency types. A strong correlation is observed across both excitatory and inhibitory populations, indicating that the TransA-MERFISH protocol did not bias or deplete neuron types in the sSC (Pearson R = 0.88). e, Validation accuracies of the XGBoost classifier trained using various gene selection strategies: the performance of the 140-gene TransA-MERFISH panel was compared to randomly sampled 140-gene sets drawn from either the full single-cell transcriptome or the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs). Additional gene sets were constructed by selecting the top k specific genes (Methods) per SC neuronal cluster (k = 1–10), based on 19 neuronal clusters identified from re-clustering of the neuronal subset of the dataset28. Data are presented as mean ± SD. f, Dot plots comparing the expression patterns of 2 non-optimal probes (top row, blue) with their corresponding expressions in snRNA-seq17 (bottom row, orange). MERFISH cells are grouped according to their predicted snRNA-seq cluster identities, as inferred by Tangram-based imputation (Methods). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Further confirmation has arrived that Markus Krösche will be joining AC Milan, and an announcement could come before the month ends.

La Gazzetta dello Sport confirm the news that been circulating for weeks now: an agreement has been reached with Krösche, and next week could be the perfect time to announce it to the world, at least as per the German director and the club’s plans.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Industry observers note that owner Gerry Cardinale made it clear that he will never again hand the club’s management over to a single executive. He will make the decisions himself, and in the summer he chose Ruben Amorim as the head coach, working closely with him and listening closely to his transfer desires.

It has been revealed that in short, he wanted to avoid introducing the traditional role of sporting director, who at many clubs decides the coach’s fate. However, the intention to strengthen Milan’s sporting side has always been there, and Krösche has always been held in high regard by Cardinale.

According to recent reports, krösche officially stepped down from his role at Eintracht Frankfurt on October 18. This separation came after five and a half years of working together, with the highlight being winning the Europa League in 2021-22.

His best acquisitions were Randal Kolo Muani (bought for free after his time at Nantes and sold to PSG for €95m), Willian Pacho (bought for €13.65m from Antwerp and sold for €40m, also to PSG), and Omar Marmoush (bought for free after a year at Wolfsburg and sold to Manchester City for €70m).

“Over the past few months, I’ve been intensely reflecting on my personal situation and my professional future,” Krösche remarked upon his departure. “I’ve come to the conclusion that I need a change. I also believe that a fresh impetus could be helpful to Eintracht.”.

The club recognised his great work: “Krösche has decisively shaped Eintracht Frankfurt. Winning the Europa League, participating in the Champions League, and the further growth of our team are testament to this extraordinary period.”.

Milan are his next chapter. Krösche will be responsible for transfer operations, likely taking the title of Head of Football. He will work closely with Head of Football Intelligence Bobby Gardiner and Head of Recruitment Tiago Estevão, key figures who enjoy Cardinale’s trust.

It has been revealed that krösche will liaise with clubs around the world and with agents. He will have a lot of responsibility, but certainly not the final say, which will rest with Cardinale after the traditional consultation with the club’s internal working group.

Above all, it will be fascinating to see what Krösche will pursue and how he will balance the pursuit of high-potential young players (his strength in Germany and a long-standing objective for Milan) with the need for short- and medium-term results.

  • Brentford striker Igor Thiago begins a three-match suspension in Monday's Premier League battle with Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium.
  • Thiago was sent off for violent conduct in the Bees' 2-0 loss to Brighton & Hove Albion before the international break, and Brentford have since failed with an appeal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 11:23, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 11:34.

Brentford striker Igor Thiago begins a three-match suspension in Monday's Premier League battle with Everton at the Gtech Community Stadium.

Thiago was sent off for violent conduct in the Bees' 2-0 loss to Brighton & Hove Albion before the international break, and Brentford have since failed with an appeal.

Thiago will therefore miss Monday's match and upcoming battles with Manchester United and Arsenal, leaving Keith Andrews to ponder two potential alternatives.

Callum Wilson is a like-for-like swap in the pure number nine sense, but the Brentford boss could alternatively deploy Kevin Schade through the middle given his abundance of wide options.

However, Schade should be stationed on the right here as Wilson is given the nod in Thiago's absence, while Keane Lewis-Potter operates higher up on the left-hand side.

Yehor Yarmoliuk was brought on for Dango Ouattara at half time against Brighton, so Andrews may be minded to go for a firm midfield three of the Ukrainian, Mathias Jensen and Vitaly Janelt on Monday.

With Aaron Hickey sidelined and Lewis-Potter potentially being utilised as a winger, El Hadji Malick Diouf could start at left-back, while Kristoffer Ajer and Sepp van den Berg are central cornerstones in Nathan Collins's absence.

Brentford possible starting lineup:.

Kelleher; Kayode, Van den Berg, Ajer, Diouf; Yarmoliuk, Janelt, Jensen; Schade, Wilson, Lewis-Potter.

‘His talent is bigger than this performance’ – De Zerbi hails goalscorer Williams-Barnett

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Soccernews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.
  • Roberto De Zerbi believes Luca Williams-Barnett's "talent is bigger than this performance" after the 18-year-old impressed on his first start for Tottenham against Ipswich Town.
  • Williams-Barnett tucked away Pedro Porro's cross in the 15th minute to net his first goal for Spurs, sending the home fans into raptures in north London.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

Roberto De Zerbi believes Luca Williams-Barnett's "talent is bigger than this performance" after the 18-year-old impressed on his first start for Tottenham against Ipswich Town.

Williams-Barnett tucked away Pedro Porro's cross in the 15th minute to net his first goal for Spurs, sending the home fans into raptures in north London.

Further chances fell to Mohammed Kudus and Jan Paul van Hecke, before Dominic Solanke struck in the 51st minute to cap off a move that once again involved Williams-Barnett, sealing a 2-0 victory for Spurs.

At 18 years and 51 days old, Williams-Barnett became the youngest player to score for Tottenham in the Premier League since Gareth Bale struck against Fulham in September 2007 (18y 47d).

And his performance has certainly left a substantial impression on De Zerbi, who had previously labelled the starlet "one of the best young players I have ever worked with.".

"He's played very well, but his talent is bigger than this performance," De Zerbi told BBC Match of the Day.

According to recent reports, "It was the first game, and I am very happy. I am very delighted with his performance, but he is a significant, big, big talent.

"The management of the younger talented players is different because you can't take risks to lose their enthusiasm and their positive mentality.

"But I think Tottenham's dressing room now is a good environment for him.

Sources indicate that "I put James [Maddison] to play very close to him to speak the same language but also to help him and put him in the best conditions to play. To play with freedom, to play with his qualities because his qualities are very big.

It has been revealed that "He's a mature guy. He is smart and understands the situation. He has great behaviour inside the group and the group is good enough to help him stay calm and to play without pressure, because he has to enjoy it on the pitch.

"He has to work hard but also he has to keep the passion to keep the love of football.".

“I am happy because he played with enjoyment, with passion, without pressure.”  Roberto De Zerbi was full of praise for Luca Williams-Barnett after today's win!

— Tottenham Hotspur (@SpursOfficial) November 21, 2026.

Williams-Barnett (18y 51d) became the sixth-youngest player to start a Premier League game for Tottenham, after Stephen Carr (17y 28d), Mikey Moore (17y 77d), Andy Turner (17y 145d), Philip Ifil (17y 270d) and Gareth Bale (18y 41d).

The youngster also became the fourth-youngest player to score on his first Premier League start, behind Daniel Jebbison in May 2021 (17y 276d), Danny Cadamarteri in September 1997 (17y 343d), and Mark Cullen in May 2010 (18y 12d).

Ipswich boss Gary O'Neil, meanwhile, admitted that his side were not at their best at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Indeed, Ipswich are now winless across their last five top-flight games, and they have conceded in each of their last 30 Premier League matches.

"We gave them a really soft first goal, which obviously gives them some comfort," O'Neil said.

Sources indicate that "And then we didn't get to our level enough today. We got into some good attacking situations, but we didn't show enough quality.

"We should have dealt with both goals better. So all in all, we can't argue with the result. They were better than us which we have to accept.".

One of Liverpool's best youngsters looks destined for an incredible promotion. This kid is the real deal and he's going to go far - quick.

Sources indicate that liverpool have some absolutely incredible young talents at the club right now, the result of a deliberate project to sign the best they could find. Rio Ngumoha is arguably still the brightest of the stars - a player who looks set to command a first-team place before long.

According to recent reports, in fact, Ngumoha creates an interesting problem for Liverpool. They've just paid enormous money to sign Bradley Barcola but he essentially plays the same role as the teenager. It's not entirely clear what the initiative is there.

Ngumoha was signed as a youth player, of course, but the Reds have gone in other directions, too. Giovanni Leoni joined for just shy of £30m from Parma in 2025. A serious knee injury sustained on his debut has kept him out since but there's reason to believe he'll be available again soon.

Ngumoha is the bright light in attack, then, while Leoni - along with Jeremy Jacquet - represents the future in defence. So what about midfield?

Trey Nyoni has been the story of Liverpool's season so far. He's stepped up not just to a regular first-team role but arguably the starting place - and he's done it in just a few months.

Virtually everyone would like the teenager to start at the base of midfield against Manchester United this Sunday and you can't really hype him more than that. The growth has been extraordinary and Nyoni looks like a world-beater talent who can dominate the Reds' midfield for years to come.

According to recent reports, his rise has been so great, in fact, that we believe he's set for a promotion next March. That's the next international break and we'd be pretty surprised if Nyoni hasn't earned himself a senior England spot by then.

This is a player who's grown from an untested teenager to a UEFA Champions League starter in three months. Give him another three or four months and he'll be considered a true star in the Premier League.

Nyoni has forced Liverpool into a difficult decision this season in regards to who starts in midfield. He's going to give them another headache in January as they weigh up the need for a latest midfielder.

Industry observers note that and now we fully expect him to give Thomas Tuchel another headache next March. We're witnessing the rise of Nyoni right now. And it demonstrates absolutely no signs of stopping soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Darren Plant | 21 Nov 2026 11:25.

Chelsea winger Mykhaylo Mudryk has continued his war of words with UAF president Andriy Shevchenko over the circumstances surrounding his failed drugs test.

Mudryk, currently on loan at Tottenham Hotspur, was given the green light to return to football in July 2026 after serving a ban of more than 18 months for testing positive for meldonium.

However, the winger did an interview earlier this week that reopened the saga, with the 25-year-old claiming that the drug could have only entered his system while on international duty with Ukraine.

Shevchenko, a former Chelsea striker and Ukraine legend, hit back at those suggestions, alleging that Mudryk wanted a UAF employee to take responsibility for his ban.

Recent findings suggest that he went as far as calling for Mudryk to retract his claims against the UAF and the Ukraine national team. Instead, Mudryk has since doubled-downed on his initial comments.

As quoted by BBC Sport, a statement read: "Neither I nor my representatives made any such request.

"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible.

It has been revealed that "In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information.

"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case.

It has been revealed that "For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong.".

Despite his previous status as Ukraine's best player, it feels unlikely that Mudryk will represent his country anytime soon.

There have been two opportunities for either Mudryk or Shevchenko to back down, but it is clear that both parties remain firm over their stance.

Mudryk is presently pushing to return from injury to feature for Spurs, his solitary appearance for the North Londoners having come in September.

Nkunku – Toe problem – October 16 to October 23, 7 days out and 1 game missed. 13. Leao – Hip problem – October 28 to October 30, 2 days out. 14. Tomori – Knee problem – October 28 to November 1, 4 days out. 15. Gimenez – Ankle problem and arthroscopic surgery – October 28, 2025 to March 21, 2026, 114 days out and 22 games missed.

  • In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a upcoming stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 10:25 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 11:32 EST, 20 November 2026.

Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada insists the team got 'fundamentally better' after this summer's transfer window, as he warned ‘spending just for the sake of it’ is not the route to putting United back on top.

In his first sit-down interview in five months, Berrada tackled topics ranging from the relationship between the Glazers and Ineos, the imminent departure of youngster JJ Gabriel, the decision not to sign a left back in the summer, as well as the decision to push ahead for a upcoming stadium despite supporter backlash on matchdays.

The United chief has been at the centre of furious protests and anti-ownership chanting at matches this season, alongside Director of Football Jason Wilcox, and he accepted that criticism of United's leadership has, mostly, been fair.

In an interview that aired shortly after latest head coach Mauricio Pochettino spoke to the media for the first time, Berrada was pressed on how much accountability falls at his door with United heading to Anfield this weekend 18th in the Premier League table.

'I think if you think about the fact we've had three permanent managers in less than three seasons, clearly we haven't achieved the stability that we wanted, that's for sure,' Berrada told Sky Sports.

It has been revealed that 'When it doesn't work out with the coach or the manager, we are all responsible. Myself, the football leadership, everyone who is involved around the coach and the staff and the players. We have to continue improving and getting better.

Manchester United's CEO Omar Berrada finally fronted up in an interview with Sky Sports.

Michael Carrick's sacking was yet another managerial change at United, with the hierarchy under massive scrutiny and Mauricio Pochettino now in the hotseat.

'There are different circumstances why it didn't work out with Erik [ten Hag], and Ruben [Amorim], and now Michael [Carrick], and we are always learning and, as I noted, trying to improve and understand what has failed.

'The challenge is we're trying to find the right manager for the squad that we have with a specific set of skills in that moment to make them perform at their best level.

In a recent development, 'It's true, we have to accept the criticism that we haven't been able to achieve that stability with one coach and our aim is to do that as soon as possible. Of course, we hope now that Mauricio coming in will give us that stability that I think we all need.'.

Berrada's links to Manchester City, where he worked prior to joining United, were brought up, not least given he worked at the club during the period that City have had charges brought against them.

'I'm not concerned,' Berrada insisted.

But at his fresh home there are problems aplenty, not least having got another managerial appointment wrong, sacking Carrick less than six months after handing him a two-year deal, and so it was put to Berrada: is the club actually progressing?

'It's not good enough, not acceptable and that's why we've made the change that we made so that we can move forward,' he concluded.

(L-R) Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Berrada and Jason Wilcox have drawn plenty of ire from Man United fans.

It has been revealed that 'But we are laying the foundations for sustained growth, to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently. It's not always been that.

It has been revealed that 'Last year we finished third, we were happy with the squad, we were happy with the way we were going. And now, a few months later, we are not where we need to be. But the foundations are there and I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction. Very positive.'.

By Ben Knapton | 21 Nov 2026 11:34, Last updated: 21 Nov 2026 11:34.

Everton manager David Moyes has confirmed that Jack Grealish is back available for Monday's Premier League showdown with Brentford at the Gtech Community Stadium.

The Manchester City loanee has missed the Toffees' last four games in all competitions due to a breach of club discipline, but he returned to action in a friendly during the international break.

Grealish has since been welcomed back to team training and is an option for gameweek 11, but the winger will surely be on the bench at best after a few weeks with no competitive minutes.

Instead, Tyler Dibling and Tyrique George should be retained in the wide areas, providing support to the two main men in Thierno Barry and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall.

Barry registered his fifth, sixth and seventh Premier League goal involvements of the season last time out, scoring two of his own and setting up Dewsbury-Hall in Everton's 3-1 win over Coventry City, but only two of his strikes have come on the road.

Further back, Harrison Armstrong and James Garner are midfield mainstays, while Moyes also has no reason to alter a backline that has conceded just five away goals this season.

Jordan Pickford's status as England number one may now be in question thanks to James Trafford's exploits, but the 32-year-old remains Moyes's undisputed first pick.

Everton possible starting lineup:.

Pickford; Rohl, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Garner, Armstrong; Dibling, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A deal has already been agreed for an African sensation who people should not forget about.

Football comes in waves. It ebbs and flows. From one generation to another. Giants are born and giants are toppled. A club like Liverpool has ebbed and flowed a lot more than others over the years.

There was a golden era in the 1970s and 1980s, followed by bleak and dark times, succeeded by even darker times on the pitch barring one miracle night in Istanbul.

Industry observers note that then along game the beacon of hope. Jurgen Klopp restored the faith at the club and took Liverpool back to the apex of the footballing world.

Now it's Andoni Iraola's job to sort out the mess he inherited from Arne Slot and follow in the footsteps of Klopp.

What Julian Ward is planning to make Liverpool the best team in the worldOf course, it's never just the head-coach who is responsible, especially these days in modern football. There's an entire operation behind Iraola. Ward sits at the helm as the club's sporting director and he has a vision to help Liverpool get back to the pinnacle. One of the club's recent recruitment strategies has been to recruit some of the best young players on the planet. This has seen Liverpool break the record for an U23 goalkeeper with the signing of Lucca Brughmanns. They have also secured the future of Djylian N'Guessan and Ifeanyi Ndukwe. This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Trips to the City Ground have rarely been easy for Arsenal, with an FA Cup defeat in January 2022, at a time when Forest were still in the Championship, sparking a famous Arteta rant in the dressing room which was included in the All Or Nothing documentary.

They were far from fluent here and have now failed to score in the first half of their last six Premier League and Champions League matches.

According to recent reports, eberechi Eze endured a particularly difficult afternoon in what was a missed opportunity for the England international, with Madueke replacing him at half-time. Yet Arteta will argue that finding a way to win games when not at their best is a sign of champions.

“We have played 11 competitive matches and won 10 of them, we are in a good place and will improve,” Arteta remarked. “Since losing at Brighton we have won three games in a row so that is the response that I want.

According to recent reports, “The level of the league has gone up again and there will be more and more surprises. We have to go again at Bayern Munich this week [in the Champions League on Wednesday night] and we will have to adapt to that one too.

“I have a smile on my face as Noni is a special guy. He’s in a good moment and after the [international] break he’s shown another level. The team needs him and he’s doing well.”.

Arsenal often struggled against teams who operate with a compact midfield and defend deeply last season and this was another case in point.

When Declan Rice wastefully lifted a shot over the crossbar 18 minutes from the end, after a rare opening in the Forest area, it did appear that another draw was inevitable.

Madueke has struggled for consistency and minutes since his £52m move from Chelsea, so this felt like a big moment for the winger.

Industry observers note that “If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd,” Madueke noted. “We have elite players of the highest level and it’s great to have that type of competition. You know on the bench that you’re ready to have an impact. We indicated grit and determination and showed a champion spirit.”.

Forest’s problems at home are increasing and Oliver Glasner is now the club’s fifth manager in a year to experience such problems. His team have now gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters. They have only recorded two home wins in the league over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Sources indicate that they did not deserve to lose this match. Without their injured talisman Morgan Gibbs-White, Forest defended resolutely and in the second half displayed far more attacking impetus without ever truly testing Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya.

Liam Delap, their £50m record signing, produced a fine centre-forward performance and never allowed Arsenal’s centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel to feel comfortable. Goals, however, continue to elude this team.

Glasner stated: “I feel really sorry for the players because we didn’t deserve that.

“It feels unfair but I don’t want to be complaining as we are the only ones who can change it.

According to recent reports, “It is a tough moment and we need to stick together and stay positive. Sometimes it takes a while – during my first year at Palace we didn’t start well but we had a turnaround.

If you look at the quality of our starting XI and bench it’s absurd so we know that we’re going to start some and finish some and for me it’s the same mentality every time I just want to create or score.

Amazing feeling [to score] but I feel better about the win.

They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Tottenham Hotspur are reportedly tracking one of French football's most prolific young players, but could face a significant financial obstacle and an unusual transfer arrangement if they pursue a January deal.

Roberto De Zerbi's side have identified Stade de Reims midfielder Yaya Fofana as a potential target, with scouts expected to attend Saturday's Ligue 2 encounter against Saint-Etienne to assess the 22-year-old in person.

According to recent reports, according to Foot Mercato, Tottenham are impressed by the Ivory Coast international's remarkable start to the season. However, Reims are unwilling to lose their leading attacking performer midway through their promotion campaign and would reportedly demand more than €25m (£22m).

The French club could nevertheless consider a deal allowing Fofana to remain on loan until the summer, potentially enabling interested teams to secure his signature without immediately removing him from Nicolas Usai's squad.

Fofana's emergence is particularly striking given that he spent more than a year on the sidelines between 2025 and 2026 after suffering a serious stress fracture.

The former Lens youngster has returned in outstanding form, benefiting from Usai's decision to deploy him further forward. Although naturally a midfielder capable of operating in defensive and central positions, he has developed into Reims' principal attacking threat.

Fofana has scored 11 goals and provided two assists in 12 Ligue 2 appearances, placing him at the top of the division's goalscoring charts despite not being a conventional centre-forward.

Sources indicate that his finishing efficiency is equally remarkable. Of his 19 shots on target, 11 have resulted in goals, while his tally considerably exceeds his expected-goals figure of 4.9. That represents an overperformance of 6.1 goals, although maintaining such clinical finishing throughout the campaign would be difficult.

Earlier this month, Fofana also received his first Ivory Coast call-up, marking another significant milestone following his lengthy injury absence.

Tottenham reportedly admire his versatility and attacking output, while Foot Mercato claims that the player is attracted by the prospect of competing in England. Saturday's encounter with Ligue 2 leaders Saint-Etienne offers Spurs' scouts an opportunity to assess him against strong opposition.

Despite the growing interest, Reims are determined to retain Fofana for the remainder of their promotion campaign.

According to Foot Mercato, the French club would not accept less than the €25m (£22m) received from Patrick Zabi's recent sale, with Fofana's performances strengthening their negotiating position.

Recent findings suggest that an immediate January departure is reportedly off the table, although a transfer followed by a six-month loan back to Reims could provide a compromise. Tottenham would secure a long-term investment, while the French side would retain a crucial player for the decisive months of the season.

Competition could complicate matters. Galatasaray have also been linked with Fofana, while Stuttgart and Trabzonspor are reportedly monitoring his progress.

Industry observers note that reims' negotiating position is strengthened by the midfielder's long-term contract. Several reports list its expiry as June 2030, although the club's most recent publicly confirmed extension, announced in November 2024, ran until June 2029.

According to recent reports, for Tottenham, scouting remains the expected next step. No offer has been confirmed, and there is no indication of an agreement with Reims or the player.

Fofana's impressive performances have made him one of Ligue 2's standout players, but Reims' insistence on keeping him until the summer means that any interested club must decide whether securing an early agreement justifies an investment exceeding £22m.

Recent findings suggest that derek McInnes can be understood in wanting a quiet January window. He’s still bonding a squad of players together. Drama and diversions are the last thing he needs when there looks to be an opportunity to win a title on the horizon.

In the case of Olwethu Makhanya, for example, this is definitely not the time to sell.

The 22-year-old South African has been impressive at centre-back, but it will take a campaign catching the attention in high-level European football for him to raise his value to Calvin Bassey levels and beyond.

Recent findings suggest that same goes for the likes of Ryan Naderi. Getting into the Czechia squad and increasing his range of experience makes him a more interesting prospect, but UEFA competition is a platform that ought to increase his premium.

McInnes, as he did this week, has to say he wants to keep his more prominent talents anyway. It would be strange to appear accepting of the board cashing in on bigger players.

It has been revealed that when it comes to Nico Raskin, however, things are different. A buyer for him should have been found in the summer after his World Cup involvement with Belgium.

Rangers midfielder Nico Raskin is an asset who could be sold in the January transfer window.

From the chit-chat around the game, it does not seem unreasonable to think Rangers maybe overvalued him in the initial part of that window and missed the boat in terms of securing a sale.

Recent findings suggest that if he stays for the rest of this season and enters the final year of his contract, though, the money you can ask for naturally reduces. The club might seek to tie him up on a latest deal, of course, but his remarks about being ‘mentally ready to leave’ at the start of the season point to the most likely direction of travel.

Is he irreplaceable? Not at all. And this is where forward planning should come into the mix.

If there’s someone out there willing to edge anywhere close to the £15m mark for the 25-year-old, they should be getting sounded out now – with a contingency plan being discussed and worked on in tandem.

Yes, Rangers need to get back to winning silverware, but the need to start raising funds through selling players – and replacing them - at appropriate times is pressing too.

As often said here, they can’t keep spending money the way they have been without considerably more coming back in return.

Raskin’s a good player, but his three-and-a-half years at Ibrox have hardly been shaped by his propensity for winning medals, have they? If a realistic fee is there in January, there’s a case to make for it being taken.

EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation.
  • Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.
  • Sources indicate that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

Sources indicate that the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

The commission has said its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has mentioned it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of new, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states remarked open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances.".

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, stated there is currently a yearslong delay in approving new pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities.".

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the issue, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation.".

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the newly introduced pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the new regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Industry observers note that pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has stated it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides.".

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, stated experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation.".

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she remarked regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she said.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, stated the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"Fresh science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel said it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a new report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which noted Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the concern.

According to recent reports, "The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring newly introduced ones to the market," Dorfmann noted.

Part of that plan, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel also supports the plan to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but mentioned it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these fresh products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

Industry observers note that "If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's crucial to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet.".

Vitor Matos has admitted that he must accept the 'anger' of Swansea City supporters after his surprise move to Strasbourg.

The Portuguese was deemed to be doing an outstanding job at the Swansea.com Stadium, a consequence of establishing the club in the top six of the Championship table.

However, despite impressing in South Wales and having a long-term contract, it became apparent earlier this week that he wanted to to move to Strasbourg in Ligue 1.

Having indicated a desire to leave Swansea after less than a year in charge, the 38-year-old has faced a backlash from fans.

Speaking at his first press conference as Strasbourg boss on Friday, Matos acknowledged that he had no issue with the reaction to his exit.

He told reporters: "One situation I need to address is Swansea. It was a really hard and tough decision to leave the club mainly because it was a place from the first day, that treated me with all respect and care – me and my family.

"So it was a really tough decision to leave and that's why I needed to thank everyone there.

It has been revealed that "Saying that, I really don't expect any good will from the Swansea supporters after my decision. I understand they are angry with that, but it's a club that I love that I worked every day to make better, me and my staff.".

Having worked under Jurgen Klopp at Liverpool, it is clear that Matos possesses coaching qualities that are appreciated in football.

However, in a managerial career spanning just 59 matches and 17 months, Matos has twice chosen to leave for positions deemed to be more appealing.

That is not necessarily a good look, and he has taken that risk for a club that have just sacked a Portuguese compatriot after 10 matches.

The argument will be that his impact at Swansea will continue to make him an attractive option going forward, but any future clubs will surely have reservations over handing him long-term contracts.
